newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: RTRS-PNG's Chan faces more army unrest over mercenaries.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-PNG's Chan faces more army unrest over mercenaries.

text.p: Papua New Guinea Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan on Wednesday faced a second wave of army opposition to his authority and to the planned use of foreign mercenaries to end an island uprising.

A senior army officer told civilian protesters in the PNG capital that the defence force was opposed to the mercenary plan and foreign soldiers detained by the army since Monday would soon leave the country.
And he said the defence force still considered Brigadier-General Jerry Singirok to be its commander -- even though he had been officially sacked by Chan.

"The mercenaries have come in here and undermined the constitutional rule of this country," Major Walter Enuma, a handgun in one hand and loud-hailer in the other, told cheering protesters outside the city's Murray barracks.
"I think they have undermined the dedication and loyalty of the soldiers and police," Enuma said.

Enuma told reporters that senior army officers were to meet shortly to decide whether the army would join a civil protest march against Chan, who on Monday sacked Singirok after the rebellious general gave Chan a 48-hour deadline to quit.
He said the army would mount a legal challenge to the sacking and in the meantime Singirok, who was still in the barracks, remained in charge.

Another senior officer contradicted Enuma, telling Reuters that the army was now controlled by acting commander Colonel Alfred Aikung. Lieutenant-Colonel Joseph Fabila said the army would not take part in any demonstration.

Enuma said 40 mercenaries from the South Africa-based private army Executive Outcomes, would be flying home. The mercenaries arrived in February to train PNG soldiers and help end the costly nine-year conflict on Bougainville, a resource-rich island northeast of Port Moresby.
"They are being looked after very well and tell their families they will be going home very soon," Enuma said.
"We are not deporting them. They are going home because we do not require their services."
The major, who also addressed troops within the barracks, said soldiers had been told to remain inside the compound.
Amid fears that the protest could be infiltrated by local criminal gangs known as rascals, as with previous demonstrations in the South Pacific nation, Enuma urged the protesters to remain calm.
"If you want to support us, you can stage a sit-in, we will not allow negative protests. Don't take action with anger...do it with love, don't do it with hate," he said.
A group of around 30 police watched the protest from across a traffic intersection. PNG's powerful police force is said to be backing Chan in the crisis.

The 40-year-old Singirok, trained in Australia and considered a battle hero from Bougainville, has vowed to carry on his campaign against the mercenaries and alleged corruption in the A$36 million (US$28 million) mercenary contract.
The plan to use the mercenaries has been condemned internationally, with Australia hinting it could withdraw valuable aid contributions to PNG.
A senior police officer told Reuters he feared the protest could end in violence, with both criminal gans and soldiers joining in the march.
"Today is make-or-break day," the officer said.
